Multiplayer matchmaking

Players press Play and wait. You must put them in a match with others nearby, with similar skill, in a few seconds. Players in a far-away region will have a bad time, so you must keep each region close. Practise this medium system design problem for free with a Google or GitHub account.

The brief

Players press Play and wait. You must put them in a match with others nearby, with similar skill, in a few seconds. Players in a far-away region will have a bad time, so you must keep each region close.

Think of finding a match in an online game.

Users, scale and requirements

Who uses it
3 million players online at peak
Audience in plain numbers
12,000,000 users or devices
Normal peak
≈ 12,000 requests per second
Request mix
Read: 55%; Write: 25%; Message: 20%
Speed for 99 of 100 requests
Read: ≈ 200 ms; Write: ≈ 200 ms; Message: ≈ 300 ms
Successful requests
99.9%
Data safety
Best effort: small losses are tolerated.
Monthly budget
≈ $32,000
Data at rest
≈ 0.5 TB
Where users are
North America: 40%; Europe: 35%; Asia Pacific: 25%
Home region
North America
Waiting deadlines
Read: 900 seconds; Write: 3,600 seconds; Message: 900 seconds

≈ marks an approximation, just as in the game. Waiting deadlines measure the age of queued work and are separate from interactive response time.

  • Each waiting player polls or holds a connection until matched (approx.).
  • Lobby messages are tiny, about 1 KB.

Questions that shape the design

How long may a player wait?

Most should be matched within 10 seconds. Being matched slowly beats being matched badly far away.

Can players play across regions?

Only when a region is empty or down. Normally keep them local: a ping above 80 ms feels bad.

Do we keep waiting tickets if a machine fails?

It is fine to lose waiting tickets. Players just press Play again.

The traffic day

Consumer traffic, busiest in the evening. The clock covers 00:00 to 24:00 in the home region. Events add pressure on top of that normal traffic.

  1. 17:00 · Overseas launch

    A launch brings users who are far from your servers.

    Affected share: 40%.

  2. 20:00 · Flash crowd

    A scheduled launch brings a sudden rush of requests.

    Traffic reaches 3 times the scheduled load; rises over 30 seconds, holds for 1,800 seconds and eases over 1,800 seconds.

  3. 21:30 · Zone outage

    An availability zone loses power or network access.

    Duration: ≈ 3,600 seconds.

What a strong design has to handle

  • Where should a player be matched: near them or in one big pool in one place?
  • Claim players into one compatible match while widening search predictably.
  • Waiting longer lets the matcher find a better skill match; matching instantly gives lopsided games.
  • Regional pools give low ping but small pools at night. You may widen the search over time.

Make a prediction, run a full traffic day, then compare the result. The in-game editorial opens after a finished day and includes measured reference designs.

Related problems

  • Medium

    Smart home

    One million homes have a hub that keeps a live connection to your cloud. The hub reports its devices every few minutes, and the phone app sends commands like "lock the door". Commands must feel instant and must not be repeated. Once in a while a power cut ends and every hub reconnects together.

  • Medium

    Notification service

    Every other team asks you to send messages: order shipped, new login, a sale starting. You send them by push, email and text through outside providers who have their own limits. Send each message once, and never block the team that asked.

  • Hard

    Scheduled job service

    Customers register jobs: "call my web address every night at 02:00" or "every hour on the hour". Aim to fire within 5 seconds; work still waiting after 60 seconds counts as failed. Retry safely after a crash. One external effect requires the customer endpoint to honor a stable job occurrence key. Half the world picks the top of the hour, so a huge crowd of jobs comes due in the same second.

  • Hard

    Video upload pipeline

    Creators upload videos that must be converted into several qualities before anyone can watch. Conversion is slow, costs real money per video, and the converter sometimes fails on a broken file. Nothing a creator uploads can be lost.
